overview.title: 📖 Overview: Which Offspring and Substitutes Actually Reach the Altar
overview.subtitle: Temurah 18a–18b
overview.hebrewSource: וְלַד שְׁלָמִים לֹא יִקְרַב שְׁלָמִים / יִקְרַב
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf finishes tracing exactly what a verse adds beyond the orally-transmitted rule that a guilt offering's substitute merely grazes rather than dies, landing on Rav Huna's teaching about an unspecified guilt offering slaughtered after being consigned to grazing. It then turns to a real tannaitic dispute: does the direct offspring of a peace offering get sacrificed as one (the Rabbis) or not (Rabbi Eliezer, fearing owners will breed entire flocks from delayed offerings)? Rabbi Shimon narrows the disagreement to only the first offspring, not further generations, and Rabbi Pappeyas testifies to the practice. Two more mishnayot follow: a thanks offering's line of offspring and substitutes counts as a thanks offering but without the accompanying bread, and a burnt offering's substitute-line counts fully as a burnt offering — except for the special case of a female designated for a burnt offering that gives birth to a male, which becomes its own dispute.

slides.title: 🐏 What Does the Verse Add to an Already-Known Tradition?
slides.subtitle: The Gemara searches for the real purpose of a limiting verse

nodes.content: ❓ We already know by oral tradition that a guilt offering's substitute grazes (rather than dies, like a sin offering's). Why then does a verse ALSO exclude it from being sacrificed?
💬 First answer: since 'grazing' and 'not sacrificed' are logically linked, this must be redundant — reconsider
💬 Second answer: the verse teaches an EXTRA consequence — one who sacrifices it anyway violates a prohibition derived from a positive mitzva

✅ Final answer (Rav Huna): the verse is needed for a different case entirely — a guilt offering consigned to graze, but slaughtered unspecified before it developed a blemish, is valid as a BURNT offering

callout.label: The verse's real payoff:
callout.text: "אָשָׁם הוּא" — 'it is a guilt offering' — teaches the animal 'remains as it is': if never consigned to graze, it CANNOT default to burnt-offering status even when slaughtered unspecified.

slides.title: 🐄 New Mishna: A Peace Offering's Own Offspring
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Eliezer vs. the Rabbis, narrowed by Rabbi Shimon
rows: The mishna's default rule from daf 17
All agree the offspring's OWN offspring is not sacrificed
The dispute is limited to the first offspring only
Testify it WAS sacrificed in practice
'We had a peace-offering cow, ate it on Passover, ate its offspring on the next Festival'

callout.label: Ambiguity remains:
callout.text: The Gemara later debates whether Rabbi Shimon's clarification means everyone agrees the GRANDCHILD-offspring IS sacrificed, or agrees it is NOT — a real dispute between Rabba and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.

slides.title: 📜 Why Would the Offspring NOT Be Sacrificed?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning shifts from wordplay to policy

boxes.title: First Attempt: A Wordplay
items: Teaches: the MOTHER may be a peace offering, not the offspring
Refuted: the same logic would wrongly exclude a thanks offering's own offspring too, contradicting an accepted baraita

boxes.title: Final Answer: A Rabbinic Decree
items: Fear: an owner might delay sacrificing his obligatory peace offering in order to breed 'entire flocks' from it for profit
Applies specifically to peace offerings, where delay is most tempting

callout.label: Underlying value:
callout.text: Even a a fully consecrated, sacrifice-eligible animal can be barred from the altar by rabbinic policy aimed at preventing economic exploitation of consecrated status.

slides.title: 🍞 New Mishna: A Thanks Offering's Line — Minus the Bread
slides.subtitle: Offspring and substitutes of a todah retain its status, with one exception
rows: Yes — 'until the end of all generations' (וְאִם עַל תּוֹדָה)
No — derived from 'עַל זֶבַח הַתּוֹדָה,' limiting the bread requirement to the original animal alone

callout.label: Derivation:
callout.text: The verse's extra 'יַקְרִיבֶנּוּ' (he shall offer IT) teaches one must choose only ONE of two recovered animals, while 'וְאִם עַל תּוֹדָה' expands the rule to cover offspring, substitutes, and replacements alike.

slides.title: 🐑 A Female Designated for a Burnt Offering Gives Birth
slides.subtitle: New mishna: substitute-of-a-burnt-offering's line vs. this special case

lines.speaker: Mishna
lines.text: A burnt offering's SUBSTITUTE line (and its offspring, forever) is fully sacrificed as a burnt offering — flayed, cut into pieces, entirely burned.

lines.speaker: But here
lines.text: If one designates a FEMALE for a burnt offering (burnt offerings must be male) and it gives birth to a male — is the male itself sacrificed, or does it merely graze until sold to fund a burnt offering?

lines.speaker: Rabbis
lines.text: It grazes and is redeemed — since the MOTHER herself could never be a valid burnt offering, being female.

lines.speaker: Rabbi Elazar
lines.text: The male offspring itself IS sacrificed as a burnt offering directly.

lines.speaker: Rava's distinction
lines.text: This explains why the mishna's FIRST clause (substitute's offspring) has no dispute at all: there, the 'mother' (the substitute) COULD be sacrificed, so even the Rabbis agree its offspring can too. Only the female-designated-for-burnt-offering case is disputed.

callout.label: A parallel challenge resolved:
callout.text: Elsewhere Rabbi Elazar seems to require even a guilt offering's leftover money to buy an individual (not communal) burnt offering — Rava limits Rabbi Elazar's lenient 'sacrifice it directly' ruling to precisely this narrow female-burnt-offering scenario.

summary.principle: A peace offering's own (first) offspring is sacrificed according to the Rabbis and testified practice, but not according to Rabbi Eliezer's rabbinic decree against flock-breeding; a thanks offering's line keeps its status minus the bread; and a burnt offering's substitute-line is fully sacrificed, except when the 'mother' herself was never sacrifice-eligible.

flowSteps.content: 🐏 The verse excluding a guilt offering's substitute really teaches Rav Huna's rule about unspecified slaughter
🐄 New mishna: R' Eliezer (offspring not sacrificed, decree) vs. Rabbis (sacrificed) — testified in practice

columns.content: 🍞 Todah's line keeps status, minus the bread requirement
🐑 Burnt offering's substitute-line sacrificed, but not a never-eligible mother's offspring

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: an offspring's eligibility for the altar tracks whether its 'parent' animal was itself ever a valid candidate for that same offering

quiz.q: According to Rav Huna's teaching, what does the verse excluding a guilt offering's substitute from sacrifice ultimately come to teach?
o: That the substitute may never be redeemed
That a guilt offering consigned to graze, but slaughtered unspecified before developing a blemish, IS valid as a burnt offering — but only if it was properly consigned first
That guilt offerings never have substitutes
Nothing beyond what was already known by tradition
quiz.e: Rav Huna teaches that the verse's real function is to validate an unspecified slaughter of a guilt-offering-consigned-to-graze as a burnt offering, while an animal never formally consigned remains disqualified even if slaughtered unspecified.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Shimon's clarification of the mishna, what is the true scope of the Rabbi Eliezer/Rabbis dispute about a peace offering's offspring?
o: It covers all future generations of offspring
It is limited to the FIRST offspring only; both sides agree about the offspring's own offspring (though what they agree to is itself debated)
There is no real dispute at all
It only concerns substitutes, not offspring
quiz.e: Rabbi Shimon states the disagreement applies only to the direct offspring; both Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis agree about the status of an offspring's own offspring — though the Gemara later debates whether that agreed status is 'sacrificed' or 'not sacrificed.'

quiz.q: What is Rabbi Eliezer's final, accepted reason for ruling that a peace offering's direct offspring is NOT sacrificed?
o: A wordplay reading 've'im' as 've'em' (mother)
A rabbinic decree (gezeirah) against owners delaying sacrifice to breed entire flocks from consecrated animals for profit
Because offspring are never consecrated at all
Because peace offerings can never give birth
quiz.e: After the initial wordplay explanation is refuted (it would wrongly also exclude a thanks offering's offspring), Rabbi Yoḥanan reattributes Rabbi Eliezer's ruling to a preventive decree against economic exploitation of consecrated animals.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna on the thanks offering (todah), how does its offspring/substitute line differ from the thanks offering itself?
o: They are not sacrificed at all
They are fully sacrificed as thanks offerings, but WITHOUT the accompanying loaves of bread
They require double the loaves
They can only be eaten by priests
quiz.e: The mishna teaches that the offspring, substitute, and replacement line of a thanks offering retains full thanks-offering status for sacrifice, but the bread requirement (unique to the original animal) does not carry over.

quiz.q: According to Rava's resolution, why does the mishna's first clause (offspring of a burnt offering's SUBSTITUTE) have no recorded dispute, while the case of a female designated directly for a burnt offering IS disputed?
o: There is no real difference between the cases

In the substitute's case, the 'mother' (the substitute itself) was itself sacrifice-eligible, so even the Rabbis agree its offspring can be sacrificed; a directly-designated female could never herself be a valid burnt offering
The substitute case involves guilt offerings, not burnt offerings
Rabbi Elazar never discusses the substitute case
quiz.e: Rava explains that the Rabbis only dispute Rabbi Elazar when the 'mother' animal itself could never have been sacrificed (a female for an all-male burnt offering); where the mother could have been sacrificed (an eligible substitute), even the Rabbis concede the offspring may be sacrificed too.
